data.title: Alibaba open-sources AI model that can detect cancer and nearly 150 conditions
data.description:
Alibaba Group Holding’s research arm, Damo Academy, has open-sourced an artificial intelligence model capable of identifying nearly 150 abdominal conditions – including cancers – by reading computed tomography (CT) scans, marking the latest step in the firm’s growing medical AI efforts.
The vision-language model, called Damo Radar, was designed to analyse contrast-enhanced CT scans covering 18 abdominal organs and identify a broad range of diseases and other abnormalities, such as malignant tumours, the institute said on Friday.
The model was trained using CT scans paired with clinical reports. In nearly 40,000 real-world examinations, it achieved an average area under the curve (AUC) of 0.913 across 146 clinical findings. An AUC of 1.0 represents perfect diagnostic accuracy.
The research team said the training method could eventually be extended to other types of medical imaging, calling the model “the world’s first expert-level generalist medical imaging model”.
In a comparative study involving 26 human radiologists from multiple hospitals, the model’s average accuracy exceeded that of 23 participants, according to the study. With the model’s help, the radiologists also managed to improve their ability to prevent missed diagnoses by 10 per cent while reducing the time required by more than 30 per cent, Damo said.
The research was published on Thursday in the journal Science. Several institutions took part in the study alongside Alibaba, including a hospital affiliated with Zhejiang University.
The model’s release builds on a string of recent medical AI advances by Alibaba as Chinese technology giants increasingly explore the use of cutting-edge technology in healthcare settings. Alibaba owns the South China Morning Post.
In recent years, Damo Academy has focused on developing AI screening tools to help doctors identify conditions including pancreatic, stomach and colorectal cancers, as well as aortic dissections.
In April, the division released the Coca AI model, which it said was more sensitive than radiologists in spotting early-stage colorectal cancer from CT scans. The model was co-developed with Chinese institutions including the Guangdong General Hospital.

data.title: Foreign carers for elderly to get 10 to 20% more pay than current helpers
data.description:
Foreign domestic carers brought to Hong Kong to look after elderly residents under a proposed government pilot scheme would receive 10 to 20 per cent more pay than existing helpers, the labour minister has said.
Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han on Friday revealed additional details about the arrangement for foreign domestic carers, as the government also released a comprehensive report outlining strategies for an ageing society.
The report listed 73 measures spanning 11 areas, many of which were revealed in the policy address earlier this week.
“The rapid development of the ageing population has an immense impact on the economy and different areas of society, and both challenges and opportunities exist,” Deputy Chief Secretary Warner Cheuk Wing-hing said.
“The government must actively formulate strategies as early as possible based on population changes and make forward-looking plans.”
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu announced in last year’s policy address the formation of a working group on ageing society strategies, chaired by Cheuk and tasked with submitting a report on the blueprint this year.
The pilot scheme to introduce foreign domestic carers, announced in the policy address on Wednesday, is among measures to tackle manpower shortages exacerbated by the greying population.
Sun said the minimum wage for carers would be 10 to 20 per cent higher than that of current domestic helpers. The carers must also receive elderly care training recognised by Hong Kong and possess at least three years of experience looking after older people.

The current minimum wage for helpers is HK$5,100 (US$654) a month.
“People can choose,” Sun said. “If you only need a foreign helper, you can continue to recruit from the foreign helpers’ market.
“But if you need someone with greater ability and they are accredited to take care of elderly people, you can pay a bit more to hire a foreign domestic carer.”
The minister added that the initiative would provide reassurance to local families seeking workers with proven experience in caring for elderly people.
Hong Kong is struggling with a rapidly ageing population. The number of people aged 65 and older is projected to increase from about 1.8 million in 2025 to 2.74 million by 2046, at which point more than one in three residents will be elderly.
Sun expressed confidence that the scheme would not disrupt the market for foreign helpers.
“If existing helpers want to change their job and become foreign domestic carers, they would need to return to their home country, receive relevant training and meet other requirements before they can come to Hong Kong,” he said.
“We do not want the newly created job causing concern to current [employers] of foreign domestic helpers.”
A government source on Wednesday said that the scheme would be launched next year.
Alice Lau Yim, permanent secretary for labour and welfare, said the carers would be required to work in a domestic setting and live with their employers, similar to the current arrangement for helpers.
“The main target is to raise the quality of foreign domestic helpers who are now taking care of elderly people and offer one more option in the market to families in need,” she said.
Currently, about 380,000 foreign domestic helpers work in Hong Kong. More than half are from the Philippines, followed by Indonesia and other countries.
But Betty Yung Ma Shan-yee, chairwoman of the Hong Kong Employers of Overseas Domestic Helpers Association, warned that the scheme could disrupt the market for domestic helpers.
She said the government had consulted employers’ groups beforehand but decided to press ahead despite opposition.
Yung noted many helpers had already undergone training before coming to Hong Kong and had been caring for elderly people for several years, making specialised carers unnecessary.
“Some dissatisfied helpers may just leave their jobs for better pay and higher status … and their flight back home [for the training] is covered by the employers,” she said.
She also highlighted the financial burden on employers, claiming that they already spent about HK$7,000 a month to cover the wages and living-in costs of helpers.

data.title: Ant International launches AI overhaul to automate global financial operations
data.description:
Ant International, the overseas affiliate of China’s Ant Group, is executing an artificial intelligence overhaul across its entire suite of global financial services, introducing AI agents designed to help manage payments, foreign exchange and treasury operations.
Described by the company as its largest-ever product upgrade, the initiative embeds AI-native solutions across all platforms: cross-border payment network Alipay+, merchant services provider Antom, account and treasury platform WorldFirst, and digital credit platform Bettr.
The global roll-out has begun and would extend through winter, the company said.
Peng Yang, CEO of Ant International, said the shift would prepare global commerce for a “fully agentised future”, adding that fintech providers needed “a future-ready trust infrastructure” paired with financial AI models and connected AI-native solutions.
The move follows a roughly US$1.2 billion series A funding round in July, backed by Ant Group, Alibaba Group Holding and other institutional investors.
Carved out as an independent operating entity in 2024, Ant International said it connects over 150 million merchants to more than 2 billion consumer accounts, processing over 25 million daily transactions across 210 markets.
The upgrade spans nearly 100 products, including AI assistants for payments and account management, tools for cash-flow forecasting, currency hedging and global payouts, and services supporting billing, tax filing, marketing and access to credit. Ant said it also introduced a business account designed for AI agents.
“We’re a problem solver for merchants,” Gary Liu, CEO of Antom, said in an interview with the South China Morning Post, noting that 89.5 per cent of Antom’s merchants already used AI agents, with 81.4 per cent of payment tasks receiving AI assistance.

Liu said agent authorisation should depend on the task and its spending limits, rather than the job titles used to determine employees’ authority. “It matters what the task is,” he said.
According to Ant International, the overhaul relies on two proprietary systems: a payment foundation model - called Antom 3-in-1 Transformer - that processes structured records, sequences of behaviour and relationships between users, merchants and devices to assess transactions, and FalconTST, a forecasting model for cash flows and currency exposures.
Ant International said FalconTST had achieved over 93 per cent forecasting accuracy and reduced corporate currency hedging and capital allocation costs by 30 to 60 per cent in real-world applications.
On top of the Antom 3-in-1 Transformer, the company built a second security layer, with a “know-your-agent” (KYA) framework linked to its Agentic Mobile Protocol, which connects mobile wallet networks to agentic transactions. The security layer includes AgentSafePay, which offers a fund-back guarantee against losses from agent-specific risks.
To combat security risks tied to autonomous transactions, the firm relies on its Antom Shield framework to guard against AI-driven fraud, as well as AgentSafePay, an indemnity scheme covering merchant losses from agent errors.
Ant International is also partnering with Visa and Mastercard to establish global agent verification standards through its Agentic Mobile Protocol.
Alibaba is the owner of SCMP.

data.title: CUHK department triggers backlash over WeChat attendance registration policy
data.description:
A department at Hong Kong’s second-oldest university has faced backlash over asking students to use mainland Chinese messaging app WeChat to register their attendance and keep its location services enabled, before later saying the arrangement was optional.
The policy was revealed after a screenshot of an email from the information engineering department at the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) was posted to the social media platform Threads on Friday.
“Starting from the next class, attendance will be recorded by scanning a QR code through WeChat. Please install the WeChat app and enable location services before coming to class,” the email said.
“Your attendance will be considered valid only if your location is detected within the classroom, such as CUHK faculty of law, CUHK Library Road, CUHK Lee Shau Kee Building.”
It added that a test QR code had been provided to students to ensure the app was working properly.
The post attracted hundreds of replies and was forwarded thousands of times.
Some students questioned online why the department had not adopted the university’s own app for checking student attendance.
The South China Morning Post has approached CUHK and the department for comment.

Other users also criticised the department and staff for using an app other than CUHK’s to track attendance and raised concerns about potential data leaks.
“Am I studying in mainland China now or what?” the author of the post, nemui._.desuyo, wrote.
The user wrote that he had already sent an email to the department to follow up on the matter and ask why it had not adopted the CUHK-developed app instead.
“How can they force us to install a third-party app just for taking attendance? Who’s going to be responsible if there’s a security breach?” another commenter said.
A user named iireneliui wrote: “CUHK has its own attendance system, plus card readers to tap student IDs. Or worst-case scenario, just use a plain old sign-in sheet. Why on earth do we have to use WeChat?”
The department later sent an email to students clarifying that they could use either WeChat or sign a paper attendance sheet in class.
“You only need to use one of these two methods. If you do not normally use WeChat, there is no need to install it just to record your attendance,” the email stated.
However, the email said students would still need to enable location services if they chose to use WeChat.
The Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data said it had not received any inquiries or complaints about the matter, adding that it would not comment on individual cases.
The privacy watchdog also said personal data should only be collected for lawful purposes directly related to a function or activity by the relevant organisation, provided the information was “necessary, adequate but not excessive”.

data.title: China’s top AI models generate just 10% of OpenAI, Anthropic revenue: report
data.description:
Chinese artificial intelligence models from seven major developers combined generate only about 10 per cent of the revenue reported for OpenAI and Anthropic, even as investor enthusiasm remains intense, according to US-based research firm Rhodium Group.
The Chinese AI models earned an estimated US$10.7 billion in annual recurring revenue (ARR) from March to August, a fraction of the more than US$100 billion combined for OpenAI and Anthropic, according to the Rhodium report published on Thursday.
The report covers DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Z.ai, MiniMax, Alibaba Group Holding, ByteDance and Kuaishou Technology, which runs the Kling AI video generator.
ARR, a widely used measure for fast-growing companies, projects current monthly subscription income over a 12-month period.
ByteDance led the Chinese group in ARR at US$4 billion as of July, followed by Alibaba at US$2.4 billion in August. By comparison, OpenAI reached US$40 billion in August and Anthropic was at US$65 billion in July.

DeepSeek and Kling had the lowest ARR among the major Chinese AI companies tracked by Rhodium, at US$500 million each as of June and March, respectively. They were followed by MiniMax at US$800 million and Moonshot at US$1 billion, both as of August.
Executives at Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, told investors on Wednesday that the company’s ARR had reached US$1.8 billion. The report stated that Z.ai’s ARR from its API business was US$1.6 billion in August.
Despite the gap, investors have continued to pile into Chinese AI companies. Rhodium said their valuations remained “substantially lower” than those of OpenAI and Anthropic, and some looked far more expensive relative to revenue.
Moonshot has been undergoing a funding round that could value it at roughly US$50 billion and has filed confidentially for a Hong Kong initial public offering (IPO), while DeepSeek was also nearing the completion of a pre-IPO funding round valuing it at about 500 billion yuan (US$74 billion), the South China Morning Post reported previously.
Meanwhile, Anthropic was expected to go public later this year with a targeted valuation of around US$2 trillion, according to media reports. OpenAI had discussed a new funding round that would value it at about US$1.2 trillion, the Financial Times reported on Tuesday.
“Valuations relative to revenue appear exorbitant for Moonshot and DeepSeek at present,” the Rhodium report said. Their estimated valuation-to-ARR multiples stood at 50 times and 163 times, respectively, compared with 34 times for OpenAI and 21 times for Anthropic.
The numbers underscore a central challenge for China’s AI industry: how to turn AI models into sustainable businesses while spending heavily to keep pace at the technological frontier.
Revenues for these Chinese AI companies have grown rapidly. Z.ai recorded a 400 per cent increase year on year in first-half revenue to 953.9 million yuan, while MiniMax’s revenue surged 283 per cent to US$116.6 million during the same period.
Still, Z.ai and MiniMax, both listed in Hong Kong, could remain loss-making through 2030 due to spending required for computing power, Macquarie Group’s head of Asia internet and software research Ellie Jiang told the SCMP last week. Investors have so far been willing to tolerate those losses while AI adoption remains at an early stage, she said.

The findings come as Chinese developers have rapidly narrowed the performance gap with their US counterparts while competing aggressively on price and embracing open-source and open-weight models.
However, the open-weight strategy has made Chinese models harder to monetise, Rhodium said. Third-party cloud providers can deploy open-weight models and sell access without paying the original developer.
“This could be changing, as Moonshot and Alibaba are pushing for revenue-sharing agreements with major users of their open-weight models,” Rhodium said. For example, Moonshot was in discussions with Microsoft, Amazon and Google, with its potential share of revenue reaching as much as 30 per cent, Reuters reported last month.
Alibaba owns the SCMP.

data.title: Asia-Pacific firms divided on how AI will impact office space demand: survey
data.description:
Nearly one-fifth of surveyed companies in the Asia-Pacific region believe wider adoption of artificial intelligence will reduce their real estate needs, a new study by CBRE has found.
More than half – 56 per cent – held a neutral view, believing either that AI had no impact on office space demand or that it was too early to determine its effect, according to the property consultancy’s poll of corporate real estate executives in the region.
The remaining 25 per cent said AI adoption would require them to expand their office footprint.
The survey was conducted between May 26 and July 10 across nine markets, including Hong Kong, mainland China, Singapore, Japan, Australia and India. It received 651 responses, with those from the mainland and India weighted more heavily to “reflect those markets’ share of Asia-Pacific grade A office stock”.
The results pointed to AI currently having a more significant impact on office operations than on real estate requirements, CBRE said.
“Although there is speculation that AI could reduce office demand, our findings suggest most organisations remain in the early stages of assessing its impact, with minimal short-term effect on real estate requirements,” said Ada Choi, head of research for Asia-Pacific at CBRE.
“At the same time, many occupiers remain confident in business growth and continue to plan for expansion. As companies rebalance their office portfolio, future growth will be concentrated in higher-quality workplaces, while lower-value space is rationalised.”
What we are seeing now is the emergence of a new equilibrium for the office market
Tom Gaffney, CBRE
AI has been blamed for lay-offs across various sectors, with lower headcounts often linked to reduced office space needs.
Last year, a study by the Switzerland-based World Economic Forum found that 41 per cent of employers across 22 industries in 55 economies planned to reduce their workforce as AI automated certain tasks.
Among CBRE respondents, 46 per cent identified themselves as AI adopters or active movers in applying AI to corporate real estate operations, up from 9 per cent in 2024.
Meanwhile, nearly nine in 10 respondents reported that employees worked in the office at least three days per week, the highest level since the Covid-19 pandemic. Another 85 per cent said office attendance had reached a steady state.
“With attendance and utilisation largely stabilised at higher levels, companies are no longer focused only on bringing employees back to the office,” said Tom Gaffney, head of leasing for Asia-Pacific at CBRE.
“They can now concentrate on transforming the workplace to improve experience and efficiency. What we are seeing now is the emergence of a new equilibrium for the office market, with companies selectively growing their portfolio and prioritising premium workplaces.”

data.title: Hong Kong to recruit AI chief by mid-2027, with confidence in local talent pool
data.description:
Hong Kong will begin recruitment for an artificial intelligence (AI) commissioner in the second quarter of next year to assist in drafting policies for the technology and risk governance, with authorities confident the city does not lack suitable talent.
Tech authorities on Friday revealed details of the new post under the Digital Policy Office, which will pay between HK$262,125 and HK$278,200 (US$33,414 to US$35,436) a month.
Permanent Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Kevin Choi Kit-ming said that recruitment for the post would begin in the second quarter of 2027.
“Their job scope will include providing their expertise and advice on various AI-related activities,” Choi said at a press briefing.
In his policy address on Wednesday, city leader John Lee Ka-chiu said that the commissioner was expected to take up the role next year and would oversee seven key areas of AI risk governance.
These include combating AI-related crimes, such as deepfake porn and online scams, and empowering authorities to remove online content linked to financial fraud.

Choi said the commissioner was also expected to be familiar with developments in the AI industry, including risk governance, global trends, its impact on public administration and its application in local industries.
Choi, who is responsible for the recruitment, said the commissioner would be hired in a recruitment exercise open to both the private and public sectors.
“I deeply believe that the development of AI in Hong Kong is not bad, so we are not worried about a lack of suitable candidates,” he said.
Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan and latest policy address placed a heavy focus on AI as a main driver of the city’s industrial transformation. “Artificial intelligence” appeared more than 190 times in the policy address alone.
Four pages were dedicated to the use of AI across eight industries to boost Hong Kong’s role as an international innovation and technology centre, including taking forward the ‘AI-plus’ initiative, a concept championed by China to integrate the technology into every sector of the economy and society.
Authorities will consult the public on strengthening the legal framework surrounding the technology and improving the detection of AI-generated fraudulent content.
The government will also review whether existing laws adequately address liability for accidents or damage caused by AI products, promote market assessment of ethical risks, step up protection for minors using the technology and ensure they use it with the proper values.
Regarding the timeline for regulating deepfake AI crimes, Secretary for Justice Paul Lam Ting-kwok noted that the cybercrime subcommittee under the Law Reform Commission was reviewing the laws, but he was unable to give a “concrete timeline” for the reform.
“Because the [commission] is an independent body comprising members from different industries, it is difficult to state definitively when a final report will be completed,” he said.
However, Lam said he understood public concerns about deepfakes, especially those involving the generation of sexual images or used in fraud. He said he would urge the commission to complete its study as soon as possible.
The new laws would incorporate maximum flexibility to prevent legislation from becoming obsolete as AI technology evolved, he added.
“Many existing laws use technology-neutral language. For example, fraud offences focus on the intent to deceive using tools, regardless of whether those tools are primitive or advanced,” he said.
Flexible “soft laws,” such as industry codes of conduct and public education, could be employed alongside legal measures, Lam added.

data.title: 3 Jellycat, Labubu plushie thieves jailed for up to 2 years and 2 months
data.description:
Three repeat offenders have been sentenced to up to two years and two months behind bars for stealing 83 Jellycat and Labubu plushies worth a total of HK$115,200 (US$14,770) from a Hong Kong shopping centre last year.
The District Court heard on Friday that the three men had stolen the popular merchandise from two claw machine shops at Kwai Chung Plaza on the instructions of other suspects who remain at large.
A waiter, Tang Lik-ming, 35, and a wood painter, Wong Wai-chun, 36, pleaded guilty to two counts of burglary for taking part in the crimes in the early hours of June 9 and June 12 last year.
Part-time warehouse worker Ho Ka-keung, 33, admitted one count of burglary for driving an accomplice to the scene during the second incident.
All three defendants had previous brushes with the law, with Ho and Wong committing the current offences shortly after they were released from prison in 2024 and 2025, respectively.
A prosecution summary of the case said Tang and Wong first met outside the shopping centre at about 3am on June 9.
Carrying four tote bags that Wong gave him, Tang used what appeared to be a stolen key to open a claw machine inside a shop on the second floor and took 23 Jellycat soft toys, each valued at HK$1,000. The two men left the scene separately 10 minutes later.
At about 5am three days later, the pair returned to the shopping centre alongside a wanted suspect to steal 60 Jellycat and Labubu from another shop on the ground floor. The plushies were worth a total of HK$92,200.

Surveillance camera footage revealed that Ho was behind the wheel of a car that took Wong to the shopping centre that morning. Police subsequently seized from the vehicle three tote bags and other items Tang used to commit the offence on June 9.
Under caution, Tang and Wong said they had agreed to take part in the scheme for a reward of up to HK$9,000.
Wong said he recruited Tang to commit the crimes at Ho’s instructions, adding that another wanted suspect had provided the keys to the claw machines to Ho in advance.
Judge Ada Yim Shun-yee said the offences were highly premeditated and all three defendants were aware of their respective roles in the scheme.
She jailed Tang for two years and Ho and Wong for two years and two months each.
Claw machine shops typically operate 24 hours a day, with staff making only occasional visits while relying on CCTV cameras to detect theft.
Burglary is punishable by up to 14 years’ imprisonment in Hong Kong.
The Court of Appeal has set 2½ years’ imprisonment as the customary starting point for sentencing burglary offences outside domestic premises, and three years for offences committed in a domestic setting.

data.title: Doctors urged to test for chikungunya as Hong Kong detects first local 2026 case
data.description:
Doctors in Hong Kong have been urged to arrange blood tests for patients with symptoms of chikungunya fever, regardless of their travel history, after the city recorded its first local case of the mosquito-borne disease this year.
The Centre for Health Protection issued a reminder to doctors on Thursday after a 55-year-old woman with no recent travel history was reported as Hong Kong’s first locally acquired chikungunya fever case in 2026.
“To facilitate early diagnosis and timely public health intervention, please consider arranging diagnostic testing for any patient presenting with symptoms suggestive of chikungunya fever, regardless of their travel history,” the centre wrote in a letter to doctors.
Testing for the mosquito-borne disease is free of charge at the public health laboratory service under the centre.
The latest infected woman, who lives on Li Tak Street in Tai Kok Tsui, started to develop symptoms such as fever, headaches and joint pain in her fingers and wrist last Monday, followed by a rash on her face and body.
She sought medical care at Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Jordan on Wednesday and was admitted on the same day for treatment. She was in a stable condition.

The woman did not travel during the incubation period, but recalled receiving mosquito bites at her residence and in areas around Cherry Street Park and Lok Kwan Street Park.
The centre is still conducting an epidemiological investigation into the case.
It urged people who had visited Li Tak Street or the two parks and exhibited symptoms such as fever, rash or joint pain to seek medical advice or contact the centre.
The woman is Hong Kong’s third confirmed chikungunya fever case this year. The first two were imported cases reported in January.
Last year, 82 chikungunya cases were recorded in Hong Kong, including 11 local cases.
Mosquito activity, as measured by the government’s Gravidtrap Index, started to pick up in some areas in Hong Kong this month.
In Sheung Wan and Sai Ying Pun, the initial index for September was 32.1 per cent, falling within the level three readings that indicated the distribution of Aedes albopictus mosquito was “extensive”.
Aedes albopictus is a type of mosquito that can spread diseases such as dengue fever, chikungunya and the Zika virus.
Aberdeen and Ap Lei Chau recorded an index of 26.9 per cent, also reaching the third-highest level in the distribution of mosquitoes under the four-tier system.

data.title: Hong Kong’s metal storage hits 30,000 tonnes in push to become global commodity hub
data.description:
Hong Kong’s push to develop into a premier gold and commodity trading hub has gained momentum, with local metal storage surpassing 30,000 tonnes, a minister has said, as the administration positions the city as the destination of choice for global capital.
Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu also said on Friday the government would expand renminbi settlement of payments for mainland Chinese services, such as buying water from the Dongjiang, in a bid to boost the globalisation of the yuan.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu rolled out an array of measures in his annual policy blueprint on Wednesday to accelerate the growth of the city’s international gold trading market, including a Joint Working Group on Commodity Trading chaired by Hui.
The government will halve the profits tax rate for qualifying physical commodity traders from the standard 16.5 per cent to 8.25 per cent by next year, and the city’s Exchange Fund, used to defend the local currency, will increase its gold portfolio.

The policies followed the launch of the trial operation of Hong Kong’s gold clearing and settlement system in July, which aims to establish the city as a major trading centre and price-setter for the precious metal.
The system is expected to begin operation officially in the first quarter of next year.
Speaking at a press conference, Hui noted total metal storage within Hong Kong’s London Metal Exchange warehouse network had crossed 30,000 tonnes, underscoring the drive to advance commodity trading.
Hong Kong has recorded robust demand for gold imports as banks and logistics companies bet on Hong Kong’s expansion of its vaults for the precious metal.
Data from the Census and Statistics Department showed about 107 tonnes of gold entered Hong Kong in July, up from 72.16 tonnes in February.
Hui noted that the trial operation of the gold clearing system had proceeded smoothly, attracting substantial deposits.
Beyond the 11 banks taking part in the trial, authorities received inquiries from other institutions interested in joining the gold trading ecosystem, which Hui described as a “good sign”.
On government payments, the policy address proposed expanding yuan payments for services rendered by mainland authorities.
Hui said the arrangements were already in place on a limited scale and described the increase as a natural next step.
He added that officials were considering paying in yuan for Dongjiang water supplies – which account for up to 80 per cent of the city’s fresh water from the Taiyuan Pumping Station in Dongguan city – as well as for training programmes run by mainland institutions.
At the same press conference, Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah revealed that authorities were liaising with more than 40 companies interested in establishing a presence in the Northern Metropolis.
“Many of them are in innovation and technology, including hydrogen energy [and] new energy development, and the other one is in quantum science, and we got another one building a logistics park,” Yau said.
To attract enterprises to the 30,000-hectare (74,130-acre) megaproject, which will feature several innovation hubs and university clusters, the government is offering tailored incentive packages featuring land-use facilitation, co-investment options and tax breaks based on operation scale.

data.title: Biomedicine powerhouse: China targets quarter of global first-in-class drugs
data.description:
China has set its sights on becoming a global biomedicine powerhouse by 2030, targeting key technological breakthroughs and at least a quarter of the world’s first-in-class drugs market under a new five-year plan for the sector.
By the end of the decade, China would “firmly rank at the global forefront” in biopharmaceutical research and development and applications, with its “core competitiveness” and international influence making a significant leap, authorities said on Friday.
The biomedical industry will emerge as a “pillar industry” for the nation, according to the pharmaceutical industry development plan published jointly by eight government agencies, including the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, the National Development and Reform Commission and the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA).
The plan sets 10 measurable targets, including requiring large pharmaceutical enterprises to generate combined revenue of no less than 3.5 trillion yuan (US$522 billion), and for the country to produce at least 50 drug makers with an annual revenue exceeding 10 billion yuan each. Sinopharm, China’s largest drug distributor, generated 575 billion yuan last year.
China’s innovative drugs market is expected to grow at an annual rate of more than 20 per cent by 2030, with at least five products achieving global annual sales of above US$1 billion, according to the plan.
Chinese first-in-class innovative drugs would account for at least 25 per cent of the global total, authorities said.
First-in-class drugs broadly refer to therapies using a completely new and unique mechanism to treat a condition, even though this is not a formal regulatory category.
The targets are significantly more ambitious than the sector’s 14th five-year plan, released in December 2021, which did not have quantifiable indicators for innovative drugs and focused on increasing R&D investment.
The push comes as China rapidly emerges as a biotech innovation force, highlighted by growing demand among Western pharmaceutical giants for Chinese-developed innovative therapies.
The total value of out-licensing deals involving Chinese innovative drugs has reached US$120 billion so far this year, up 36 per cent from a year earlier, news agency Xinhua said earlier this week, citing NMPA data.
The latest plan also calls for “systematic breakthroughs” in core technologies across “critical fields”.
In a report published earlier this month, Xinhua Think Tank Research, a journal under the state-run news agency, identified cell and gene therapy, green manufacturing of chemical drugs, biomedical big data and synthetic biotechnology as among key areas.
China should also expand the use of artificial intelligence, quantum computing, and supercomputing in pharmaceutical R&D, while deepening the application of frontier technologies like gene editing and brain-computer interfaces, according to the government agencies.
The plan outlines several critical areas requiring breakthroughs, including artificial life system synthesis, organoids and organ-on-a-chip, as well as universal cell therapies.

data.title: Hong Kong talent schemes could add 1.2% to GDP annually, John Lee says
data.description:
Talent attracted to Hong Kong under various admission schemes could add about 1.2 per cent to the city’s gross domestic product (GDP) each year, the city leader has said, adding that more than half of those reaching the three-year mark are willing to stay.
Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu said on Friday the government had attracted more than 300,000 people through its talent measures, with about 20 per cent from places outside mainland China.
“These talent will create an extra GDP of probably 1.2 per cent every year because they are very well qualified,” Lee told a phone-in radio programme, days after delivering his policy address and unveiling the city’s first five-year plan.
“They can do jobs that will receive higher pay and will reflect the contribution they can make to the economy.”
He said the government reviewed the status of admitted talent from time to time and found that most intended to remain in the city.
“We have a plan of examining their stay, whether we should continue [their visa], after three years,” he said. “And so far, more than 50 per cent of them are willing to continue.”
A supplement to the recent policy address showed that more than 61,000 extension applications under various talent admission schemes were received between January and August this year, with about 58,000 approved.
The government had earlier set a target of approving at least 50,000 extension applications annually between 2025 and 2027.
Lee linked the talent drive to Hong Kong’s manpower needs, noting that the city recorded a natural population decline of about 20,000 people annually.
The city’s population stood at around 7.5 million after rising by about 19,000, despite deaths outnumbering births by around 20,000 annually, he said.

Hong Kong’s population is expected to remain flat over the coming years, with only minor increases supported by talent schemes, imported workers and one-way permit holders from the mainland.
Lee said that even when the population increased, it would be just a “very moderate” upward trend.
He added that the labour and welfare authorities would release an updated manpower projection soon to determine how many more people the city needed to attract.
A projection conducted in 2023 indicated Hong Kong would face a shortage of about 130,000 workers by 2028, Lee said.
He warned that the shortfall could reach around 300,000 without new talent arrivals.
The government will consider adding more artificial intelligence-related professions to the Talent List, which currently covers 60 occupations facing local manpower shortages, according to the policy address supplement.
Authorities will also relax extension requirements under the Top Talent Pass Scheme for some technology start-up operators in the first half of next year.
Lee said he had originally set a target of attracting 30,000 people annually when the government expanded its talent drive four years ago, but did not intend to raise it despite exceeding that goal.
“If [talent] doesn’t join my side, they join the competitor’s side,” he said. “So when you have this competition game, I have to ensure that Hong Kong has the best people.”

data.title: Chip foundries better shielded in AI slowdown than Asia-Pacific tech peers: S&P
data.description:
As market fears mount over waning Big Tech spending and calls to slow down frontier artificial intelligence development, Asia-Pacific semiconductor foundries are better positioned to withstand a potential downturn in AI investment than other tech hardware firms in the region, according to S&P Global Ratings.
In a report published on Thursday, the rating agency said it had stress tested four key Asia-Pacific sectors – foundries, memory manufacturers, cooling component suppliers and original design manufacturers that assemble servers – against two downside scenarios for the AI boom.
The first possibility involved a drop in capital expenditure from major hyperscalers like Amazon and Microsoft. The second stemmed from bottlenecks that could delay AI projects, such as power grid constraints and land scarcity.
Under both scenarios, contract chipmakers, which manufacture chips for semiconductor designers such as Nvidia, were expected to prove the most resilient. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world’s largest foundry, was highlighted as particularly well insulated due to its dominant lead in advanced manufacturing.
The findings underscore how top regional foundries were uniquely positioned to shrug off temporary spending lulls.
Behind TSMC and second-ranked Samsung Electronics, mainland Chinese players hold significant market share. Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp (SMIC) and Hua Hong Group ranked third and sixth globally by revenue in the second quarter this year, according to research firm TrendForce.
By contrast, memory chipmakers such as Samsung and SK Hynix could face more pronounced earnings declines if investment appetite peaked early, the report noted.
“Rated Asia-Pacific tech-hardware issuers maintain sufficient buffers against delays in AI spending plans,” said S&P analyst Clifford Kurz, though he cautioned that a fundamental shift in long-term AI demand could still pose credit risks.

The report comes amid heightened nervousness on Wall Street and other markets, where an AI-driven stock rally is facing fresh scrutiny. Prominent US industry leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, have recently urged the sector to temper its breakneck pace of advancement to establish safety guardrails.
While some analysts believe clearer rules would be beneficial for the industry in the long run, the proposed pause has unnerved some investors accustomed to aggressive buildouts.
Capital expenditure by China’s major tech companies was set to more than double to around US$140 billion this year – up from US$65 billion in 2025 – and reach US$165 billion by 2027, according to a Moody’s report earlier this month.
Meanwhile, five major US hyperscalers – Microsoft, Amazon Web Services, Alphabet, Meta Platforms and Oracle – alongside AI cloud provider CoreWeave, were projected to spend more than US$785 billion this year alone, approaching US$1 trillion by 2027.
S&P maintained its base-case forecast that demand across the AI value chain would remain strong over the next two years.
In a separate report released on Thursday, S&P noted that mainland China’s AI buildout would disproportionately enrich a handful of top-tier cities.
Shanghai, Beijing, Shenzhen and Hangzhou were set to reap the biggest gains due to their dense pools of research talent, established engineering bases and deep capital reserves, according to the report.
“Benefits will reach the places best equipped to host firms building out related infrastructure and services. The rest of the country will have to hope and wait for second-order effects,” the agency wrote.
Shanghai’s dominant position is already evident. Official data showed that the city’s three frontier industries – integrated circuits, biopharmaceuticals and AI – had surpassed 2 trillion yuan (US$298.5 billion), with its chip sector alone accounting for roughly a third of China’s national total.

data.title: Double blow as top HSBC bankers lose education perk as job risks mount: sources
data.description:
Senior bankers at HSBC are facing a double blow of losing a key employment benefit while also confronting potential job losses as the lender carries out a range of measures to cut costs and achieve fair treatment for all staff, according to sources.
HSBC, the biggest lender in Hong Kong, will scrap an education subsidy programme for all newly hired or newly promoted senior executives from Friday, according to an internal memo seen by the South China Morning Post.
Employees who were already in the bank’s top three grades as of Thursday, including managing directors and department heads, will continue to enjoy the benefit, which provides subsidies of up to HK$300,000 (US$38,240) for secondary school fees and HK$220,000 for primary school fees per year.
“It is a double blow to management like me as we are seeing more benefit cuts while also being among those most likely to lose our jobs in the current restructuring and integration of back-office teams between HSBC and Hang Seng Bank,” a source said.
HSBC, which completed a US$14 ­billion buyout of shares it had not yet owned from subsidiary Hang Seng Bank in January, has recently begun integrating seven back-office functions across the two lenders. The functions are corporate communications, company secretaries, compliance, information technology, internal audit, finance and operations.
“After the integration, six of the seven combined units are headed by Hang Seng Bank executives and only one by HSBC,” the source said. “It is really scary because I do not know if I will still have a job tomorrow.”
Another HSBC source said the moves were aimed at reducing costs while ensuring fair treatment for global staff.
“It should be noted that neither Hang Seng Bank nor HSBC’s operations in other markets offer education benefits, with Hong Kong being the exception. The bank has discussed cutting these benefits for several years,” the source said.
“The arrangement allowing Hang Seng Bank executives to lead most of the combined back-office functions also shows a fair approach that gives opportunities to both HSBC and Hang Seng Bank.”
While some bankers may be concerned about the changes, shareholders appear to have taken a different view.
HSBC’s strong share-price performance suggests investors have broadly supported CEO Georges Elhedery’s strategy since early last year of streamlining global operations to reduce costs by US$1.5 billion. That target was achieved in the middle of 2026, six months ahead of schedule.
“It is definitely a good move for HSBC to integrate with Hang Seng Bank to reduce excess staffing, unnecessary spending and costly benefits because that could help profitability. There is no point maintaining two separate large teams to do the same job,” said Charles Cheng Kai-min, who has been an HSBC shareholder for more than 20 years.
“I am very happy with HSBC’s share-price performance because the value of my holdings has risen more than 50 per cent over the past year – thanks to the bank’s cost-cutting measures.”
HSBC shares rose 2.3 per cent to HK$163.40 by 2pm on Friday. The stock has risen 53 per cent over the past year, outperforming the Hang Seng Index, which gained 3.6 per cent during the same period.
HSBC co-CEOs for Asia and the Middle East, David Liao Yi-chien and Surendra Rosha said in Thursday’s internal memo that the lender would continue to invest in talent.
“We’re investing in our people, providing competitive, fair and inclusive benefits that reward high performance while supporting our long-term growth ambitions,” the co-CEOs said.
“We want to be intentional about how we allocate resources and will invest in benefits and support that are accessible to a wide range of colleagues.”
An HSBC spokesman said on Friday that the bank remained focused on “rewarding our employees fairly and competitively”.
He added: “HSBC employees in Hong Kong have access to a broad and market-competitive total rewards package.”

data.title: China to see major shift to Huawei for AI model training in 2027: rotating chair
data.description:
Huawei Technologies expects a major domestic shift towards its artificial intelligence computing infrastructure for model training next year, as its Ascend processors gain ground on Nvidia in China despite supply constraints, according to rotating chairman Eric Xu Zhijun.
“I believe that starting from next year, a lot of the AI model training will be based on the SuperPoD or SuperCluster based on Ascend 950DT,” Xu told reporters during the Huawei Connect 2026 conference in Shanghai on Thursday.
Xu said Huawei’s proprietary Ascend chips had overtaken Nvidia in domestic market share, although he did not provide specific figures.
Nvidia confirmed last month that it had begun shipments of its H200 processors to China under a new US licensing arrangement after a months-long lockout, although those sales represented less than 1 per cent of its second-quarter data-centre revenue.
Huawei has been pushing its own alternative computing infrastructure amid US export controls that were designed to restrict China’s access to advanced semiconductors, such as those from Nvidia.
China’s most advanced AI models were still being trained on Nvidia chips, the SCMP reported last month, citing sources at major Chinese AI developers.
“Even though there might be some gaps between Ascend and some of its competitors, it offers the strongest support for mainland Chinese customers,” Xu said, adding that many clients chose Ascend due to geopolitical risks and a preference for multi-vendor strategies.
“Pushing full chip self-sufficiency is the certain path forward for China,” Xu said. “I believe it will become a reality sooner or later.”

However, international availability for Huawei’s latest hardware remains constrained.
While the Shenzhen-based tech giant unveiled its new Atlas 960 SuperPoD computing cluster on Thursday – powered by Ascend 960 chips and boasting double the training and inference performance of its predecessor – production limits would keep the systems mostly within China, Xu said.
“Since we don’t have enough capacity to even satisfy the demand in China, we don’t have the plan to expand [SuperPoD systems] to the international market in a fully fledged way,” Xu said, though he noted the firm has been shipping small quantities overseas for testing in high-demand regions.
Huawei’s previous-generation Atlas 950 SuperPoD, powered by the Ascend 950DT chip, had increasingly been deployed for AI model training with encouraging initial testing results, according to Xu. Huawei had deployed over 1,000 Atlas SuperPoD units across more than 370 enterprise customers, the company said.
On Thursday, Huawei also introduced its Peerium Computing Architecture, a technology designed to interconnect 1 million processors to function as a single computer. Already deployed on Atlas 950 systems, Peerium was undergoing testing on the new Atlas 960 hardware, the company said.
Despite its technological leaps, Xu cautioned that computing supply still lagged behind China’s surging AI demand. He projected that global AI computing supply and demand would reach equilibrium around 2029, with China reaching a balance slightly later in 2030.

data.title: ByteDance spin-off Anew Labs raises US$290m amid AI drug design fundraising boom
data.description:
China is seeing a fresh fundraising boom for artificial intelligence-powered drug developers, with start-ups including a ByteDance spin-off raising hundreds of millions of dollars this week as investors rush to back domestic challengers to Anthropic and Isomorphic Labs.
Anew Labs, a Shanghai-based AI drug discovery firm and former unit of Chinese tech giant ByteDance, has raised US$290 million at a valuation of US$1.5 billion, according to an informed source.
Investors included prominent venture capital firms such as HSG – formerly Sequoia China – IDG Capital and 5Y Capital, the source said, with ByteDance maintaining a 56 per cent stake.
Anew Labs, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment, operates a range of AI models for biomolecular structure prediction and design. They include AnewFold, its in-house foundation model, and Protenix, an open-source reproduction of AlphaFold 3, the most advanced biomolecular prediction AI model from Google DeepMind and its Isomorphic Labs spin-off.
The Chinese company said on its website that it has four drugs in its development pipeline, including an oral small-molecule drug for immunological diseases. On Thursday it launched its AnewDDE agentic platform, which it said was designed to address “fragmented” AI workflows in drug discovery.
AI’s role in drug design is advancing rapidly. Danish pharmaceutical giant Novo, formerly Novo Nordisk, announced a partnership with Anthropic on Wednesday, saying it would use the US AI firm’s models and its Claude Science platform to accelerate the discovery and development of new medicines.


Anthropic said in June that its Mythos 5 model, only available to selected partners, made aspects of the drug design process around 10 times faster. The company said last month that its Claude Mythos Preview and Opus 4.8 models had designed protein binders from scratch that succeeded against 14 of 15 targets.
Start-ups in China have ramped up their fundraising efforts.
Nutshell Therapeutics, a Shanghai-based biotech firm focused on developing small molecule drugs with AI, said on Tuesday that it had raised tens of millions of US dollars in a C+ round, with backers including Citic Capital, Decheng Capital and state-backed Fortune Venture Capital.
With nearly 20 planned drugs in its pipeline, the company’s lead programme targeting tumours was advancing through phase one and two clinical trials in the United States and China, it said on its website.
Beijing-based AI drug discovery firm AIPher, started in July and incubated by Tsinghua University’s Institute for AI Industry Research, said this week that it had completed an angel round of financing worth about 100 million yuan (US$14.9 million).
The start-up’s fastest-progressing pipeline, targeting attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, is in the pre-preclinical candidate stage, according to an article published on its official WeChat account on Monday.

data.title: Hong Kong IT analyst charged with murdering wife at their flat
data.description:
A Hong Kong IT analyst has been remanded in custody after being charged with killing his wife in a flat at a private residential estate two days ago.
Wong Chi-kwong, 51, was brought to Eastern Court for the first time on Friday to face a count of murder.
Police arrested him on Wednesday after his wife, 53-year-old Wong Yuk-ting, was found dead in a flat in block 2 of Heng Fa Chuen estate in Chai Wan.
The defendant appeared composed in the dock when the murder charge against him was read out.
He told the court he understood that he was accused of killing his wife and that he now faced criminal proceedings.
Prosecutors asked for a 12-week adjournment for further investigation. Their request was granted by Principal Magistrate David Cheung Chi-wai, who set the next hearing for December 11.
Police on Wednesday said the wife was confirmed dead at the scene.
Heng Fa Chuen is a private waterfront residential estate built directly above the MTR depot in Hong Kong’s Eastern district.
Developed in the 1980s, the self-contained community has 48 residential towers and a shopping centre.

data.title: China’s Z.ai raises revenue target 25% after US$5 billion cash injectionThe AI firm said its computing power bottleneck was no longer a ‘primary constraint’ thanks to its fresh US$5 billion war chest.
data.description:
Chinese artificial intelligence developer Z.ai has raised its year-end annual recurring revenue (ARR) outlook by 25 per cent to US$3 billion, as the firm indicated its fresh US$5 billion war chest had helped clear its computing capacity bottlenecks for the time being.
The updated ARR projection, up from a previous estimate of about US$2.4 billion, was disclosed during an investor call on Wednesday, according to a transcript seen by the South China Morning Post.
The revised guidance comes days after Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, announced it had raised US$5 billion through a share placement and convertible bond sale. The firm will use the funds to expand its computing power to support the training of new models and meet a surge in demand for its AI services.
Z.ai’s ARR – a key metric projecting a firm’s monthly subscription income over a 12-month period – had reached US$1.8 billion so far this year, executives said during the call. “In the short term, computing power supply is no longer the primary constraint on the company’s rapid revenue growth,” they added.
The company’s shares rose 5.9 per cent to close at HK$720 in Hong Kong on Wednesday, helping to offset a combined loss of 14.3 per cent over Monday and Tuesday amid a global slump in AI-related stocks. Despite recent stock volatility, the firm is still trading at more than six times its January listing price.
The easing of the firm’s computing constraints marks a turnaround from earlier this year, when Z.ai was forced to temporarily suspend sales of its Coding Plan after the release of its GLM-5 model in February, due to a shortage of computing reserves.
Momentum appears to have picked up since then. Z.ai’s coding user base expanded by more than 1 million in the two weeks following the release of its first-half results in late August, the company said.


Management also said a planned 30 billion yuan (US$4.5 billion) infrastructure push could add up to 100,000 petaflops of computing power, with 40 per cent reserved for model training and research and the remaining 60 per cent for inference.
That inference capacity could generate as much as 40 billion yuan in annual revenue, executives said, while cautioning that actual returns would depend on factors including utilisation, customer discounts and computing costs.
On AI applications, Z.ai said its co-working tools were gaining traction beyond coding products. Industry orders had exceeded 1 billion yuan since the launch of GLM-5.3 in August, with about 100 cybersecurity companies integrating GLM models into their products and workflows, it said.
The Beijing-based company is also expanding commercialisation beyond direct application programming interface (API) sales. It has signed revenue-sharing agreements with several major domestic and overseas cloud service providers, with related revenue expected to be recognised from October, according to company executives.
In August, Z.ai reported a 400 per cent increase in first-half revenue to 953.89 million yuan, driven by explosive growth in its open platform and API business. The extra revenue helped the firm narrow its total loss for the period by 12.1 per cent to 2.07 billion yuan, despite higher research and development spending.

data.title: China opens Pinglu Canal; Hong Kong unveils first 5-year plan: 7 highlights
data.description:
We have selected seven stories from this week’s news across Hong Kong, mainland China, the wider Asia region and beyond that resonated with our readers and shed light on topical issues. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing.
1. China launches Pinglu Canal, slashing transit time to Southeast Asia
China officially opened its landmark Pinglu Canal to navigation on Wednesday, creating a new maritime gateway for the country’s southwestern hinterland and providing a shorter route to Southeast Asia as Beijing seeks to deepen trade with the region.
2. Chinese defence chief skirts flashpoints at Xiangshan Forum ahead of Xi-Trump summit

With just a week to go until Chinese President Xi Jinping heads to Washington for his first state visit in more than a decade, Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun opted for the diplomatic path in his address to China’s premier security conference on Wednesday.
3. Hong Kong sets 5-year plan to double innovation spending, boost new industries
Hong Kong’s leader has unveiled the city’s first five-year blueprint, aligned with China’s national development strategy, setting targets to nearly double innovation spending and raise the share of manufacturing and new industries to 5.5 per cent of the economy.
4. Has a Chinese DF missile been used for the first time in the Middle East?

Debris from a Chinese-made short-range ballistic missile has been found in Yemen for the first time, suggesting Chinese weapons systems may have been used during the heated conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.
5. Hyrox Beijing athletes get full refund, new rule on hygiene risks comes into force
Hyrox China has given full refunds to competitors affected by last weekend’s incontinence incident in Beijing, while the global governing body has updated its rule book to allow race directors to remove athletes if they pose a risk to the hygiene of the event.
6. South Korean killer’s drone escape from Philippine prison foiled by test footage

A South Korean crime lord convicted of murder in the Philippines reportedly planned to escape prison by strapping himself to a drone – until his own accomplice’s rehearsal footage gave the game away.
7. Knife attack in China’s Guangzhou leaves multiple people injured
Police in Guangzhou said on Monday they had apprehended a man in the southern Chinese city’s university town district after receiving reports that he was wielding a knife and injuring pedestrians.

data.title: In Focus|China’s rocket recovery was a space race milestone. Is a relaunch within reach?
data.description:
As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the second part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Ben Jiang examine the country’s strategy and progress on reusable rockets – a field where the US has a tremendous lead.
US commercial space firm SpaceX has been eager to tout its deployment of reusable first-stage rocket boosters, claiming to have flown more than 600 missions with the cost-cutting launch components.
Despite a succession of breakthroughs in booster-recovery efforts in recent months, both on land and at sea, China has yet to reuse one – a stark contrast laying bare the gap between Beijing’s space ambitions and the challenges that remain.
Last month, Chinese private aerospace company LandSpace landed the booster of its Zhuque-3 rocket on deployable landing legs at a site in the northwestern province of Gansu, marking the country’s first successful ground-based controlled recovery using landing legs, an approach that closely resembles that of SpaceX’s Falcon 9.
The significance of landing a launched rocket goes beyond the spectacle of bringing a booster back intact, according to industry experts.
Rocket reuse was “essential for achieving low-cost, frequent and sustainable [launches] … and providing new opportunities for large-scale commercial space exploration”, a team from three major Chinese aerospace research institutions said in a paper published in March.
LandSpace said the first stage represented “about 70 per cent” of a rocket’s cost, with reuse able to spread that expense over multiple missions, underscoring the cost advantages of reusing first-stage boosters.
Some Chinese launch services can cost around US$20,000 per kilogram (about US$9,070 a pound) of payload, compared with roughly US$2,700 to US$3,000 for SpaceX’s reusable Falcon 9, according to a report published by the Mercator Institute for China Studies in February.
The large gap helps explain why rocket makers are racing to develop vehicles that can be recovered and reused.
The Chinese paper from March said there were several different approaches to bringing a rocket back, including recovery using parachutes or wings to slow the vehicle for a safer arrival.
Other approaches include landing leg recovery, with the booster using its engines to control its descent before touching down vertically on deployable landing legs.
While China still lags behind the US in landing leg recovery, it is also betting on a different approach to booster recovery: an offshore net-capture system that uses a recovery vessel to catch the descending booster.
In July, it successfully retrieved part of a Long March-10B reusable rocket following its maiden launch by using a unique sea-based net-capture system for the first time.
Compared with the landing leg recovery approach, net-capture had relatively less demanding requirements for the booster’s final landing-point accuracy, avoided the need to install heavy landing-support structures on the rocket and allowed the offshore recovery platform to be deployed flexibly, Wang Long, the founder of space technology consultancy Nihao Taikong, was quoted as saying in a report by Shenzhen-based Securities Times in July.
Hao Jinjie, an engineer at China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation, told state broadcaster CGTN the net-capture method was “like dropping a pen from the 100th floor into a pencil holder, while keeping its speed and orientation under control”.


China’s pursuit of reusable rockets draws on both its state aerospace groups and its ability to mobilise the private sector behind national priorities through the deployment of industrial policy.
Galactic Energy’s kerosene-fuelled Pallas-1 reached orbit earlier this month, with a recovery attempt deliberately deferred to later missions. The rocket is designed to carry up to 7 tonnes to a low-Earth orbit, intended for use on the first stage of at least 25 flights.
ISpace flew the same low-altitude methane demonstrator twice in 2023, though its orbital SQX-3 has yet to launch. Space Pioneer, Orienspace, Deep Blue Aerospace and Space Epoch also have reusable rockets at various stages of testing or development.
To make reusability economically viable, a booster needs to be able to re-enter space and survive repeated launches. Dai Zheng, chief commander of the Zhuque-3 missions at LandSpace, said those were areas in which China had little experience.
China had no established technical framework covering rocket reuse standards, inspection procedures or rules governing component replacement, Dai told state broadcaster CCTV in an interview last month.
“China has just solved the question of whether a rocket can come back,” he said, adding that there was “no system yet for determining whether a recovered rocket can fly again”.
In a research report published last month, analysts at Jinyuan Securities emphasised that a reusable rocket required a complete post-recovery processing cycle, including safely draining and disposing of residual propellant, isolating potential hazards and conducting non-destructive inspections of the vehicle’s structure, welds and propellant tanks.
Other necessary steps involved assessing the remaining life of engines after repeated thermal and pressure cycles, replacing worn components such as seals and valves, and carrying out system-wide functional tests before another flight.
LandSpace has said it plans to reuse the Zhuque-3 booster recovered last month in a space mission in the next six months, while the China Academy of Launch Vehicle Technology has said it aims to conduct a reuse flight of the first-stage Long March-10B by the end of this year.
Success in those endeavours would mark a crucial shift for China from demonstrating that it can recover a booster to proving that it can fly one again – essential to realising its commercial space ambitions.
A decade ago, a central government white paper called for research into low-cost launch vehicles and reusable transport systems capable of travelling between Earth and space.
Recovery and reuse are the central technologies for lowering the cost of putting each kilogram into orbit and increasing launch frequency
Xu Ying, GalaxySpace
What began as a research objective has moved through engineering trials and become a national industrial push. China’s latest five-year plan made building the country into a “space power” a priority, and specifically mentioned the development of reusable launch technology, including a reusable heavy-lift launcher for deep-space programmes.
Every serious ambition China has in space – from constellations of broadband satellites to orbiting computing networks and missions to the moon – will depend on reusable launch systems.
“Recovery and reuse are the central technologies for lowering the cost of putting each kilogram into orbit and increasing launch frequency,” said Xu Ying, general manager of public affairs at satellite manufacturer GalaxySpace. Only then, she added, could “space infrastructure” be deployed at scale and become commercially viable.
China’s two flagship broadband projects show the size of the task. China Satellite Net plans for its Guowang constellation to have 12,992 satellites, with roughly 1,300 scheduled to be in orbit by 2029 and the full network deployed by 2035.
Shanghai-based SpaceSail’s Qianfan network is aiming for more than 15,000 by 2030, but the two Chinese companies combined have less than 500 satellites in orbit at present – around 4 per cent of Starlink’s orbiting fleet of more than 11,000.
LandSpace launched 10 Qianfan satellites into orbit on Tuesday, marking the first deployment for a large-scale satellite internet constellation by a private Chinese rocket company. Another eight were launched on Wednesday.
SpaceSail aims to expand the Qianfan constellation to 324 satellites by the end of the year – up from 256 at present – leaving a narrow window of just over three months to launch 68 more.
A space industry researcher based in Xian, capital of northwestern China’s Shaanxi province, said some experts were optimistic that China would be able to make steady progress in the reusable rocket race.
He said that while SpaceX – founded in 2002 – had a head start in many aspects of the commercial space sector, Chinese companies were making progress. However, he added, China’s industry might encounter difficulties due to a comparative lack of experience in advanced rocket engines, as “no one from outside China would teach you how to design them”.
Engines accounted for more than 50 per cent of the total cost of a rocket, Wang Zijing, an analyst at Soochow Securities, wrote in a research note issued this month.
Jinyuan Securities said engine life and repeated ignition were among the biggest technical challenges in the reuse of boosters.
A reusable booster must restart its engines during ascent, re-entry and landing and operate reliably across a wide range of thrust levels, meaning that key components including its turbopumps, combustion chamber, nozzle and valves must be able to withstand repeated thermal and pressure cycles as well as vibration loads.
No Chinese rocket engine has yet made a second orbital flight. Meanwhile, a SpaceX Falcon 9 booster was sent into space for the 37th time last month.
“Reusable technology remains a new field that requires continued learning,” Lou Luliang, the chief designer of the Long March-10B, told Beijing-based China Aerospace News in a report published in July. “The thermal and mechanical conditions during an actual return, component damage and the patterns of reuse cannot all be fully understood through ground testing alone”.
